title: An item id is used as a file path without validation

sections.heading: Why
sections.body:
`ids.allocate` checks that an id is unique and nothing else. The id then becomes a
filename: `store.slice_path` joins it onto `.slicer/slices/`, and `promote` writes there.
Nothing between the two rejects a separator or a parent reference.

    $ slicer add "escapee" --id '../../../pwned'
    $ slicer promote '../../../pwned'
    promoted ../../../pwned -> .../proj/.slicer/slices/../../../pwned.json

That file lands three levels above the tracking directory — outside the project. A
gentler one, `--id 'S/1'`, silently creates `.slicer/slices/S/1.json`, a subdirectory the
loader does not scan, so the slice becomes invisible while the index still claims it
exists. `slicer check` passes on both.

**This is not only reachable through `--id`.** `legacy._parse_row` returns whatever sits
in the first table cell as the item id, with no character rule:

    >>> legacy._parse_row('| [../evil](../evil.md) | t | M | x | f | done |', ...).item_id
    '../evil'

So `slicer migrate` pointed at a markdown tree someone else wrote can write outside the
project. The docs actively encourage migrating an existing tree, which makes that a
realistic path rather than a theoretical one.

Filed at M rather than S because the fix has to cover three entry points and decide what
happens to a project that already contains a bad id.

sections.heading: Files
sections.body:
- `src/slicer/ids.py` — `allocate`, and a character rule to share
- `src/slicer/store.py` — `slice_path`, as the last line of defence
- `src/slicer/migrator.py` — ids adopted from a legacy tree
- `src/slicer/verify.py` — report an id already stored that breaks the rule

sections.heading: Failing tests
sections.body:
1. `Add_IdWithASeparator_IsRefused`, for `/` and `\` and `..`.
2. `Add_IdWithMarkdownPunctuation_IsRefused` — `|`, `]`, `(`, `)` break the Slice cell's
   link even though S21 keeps the row well-formed.
3. `SlicePath_IdEscapingTheSlicesDirectory_IsRefused` — the belt-and-braces check, so a
   hand-edited index cannot do it either.
4. `Migrate_TreeWithATraversingId_RefusesToWrite`.
5. `Verify_StoredIdBreakingTheRule_IsReported`.

sections.heading: Implement
sections.body:
One rule in `ids`: `[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*`, never containing `..`. `is_valid` for
callers that report, `require_valid` for callers that refuse, raising
`StateError(code="bad_id")`.

Enforced at seven sites, not the three this slice originally named. The audit found four
more, two of which bypass everything the slice covered:

- `ids.allocate`, on the explicit id **and the generated one** — a hostile `id_prefix`
  makes every generated id traversing, so the generated side needs it too.
- `Config.validate`, on the prefix, so that failure lands at load.
- `store.slice_path`, the main write boundary.
- `migrator.build`, on the table row id **and separately on the slice file's H1 id** —
  `legacy.H1_RE` is `\S+`, and the H1 id is the one `migrator.write` uses as a filename.
- `migrator.write`, which has its own join and never goes through `slice_path`.
- `render.plan`, which has its own join; `render.write` mkdirs parents, so a bad id
  escaped `.slicer/render/` too.
- `verify.offline`, reporting an id already stored.

**Not at lookup.** `Index.get`/`require`/`position` stay as they are: `S99` is the
canonical nonexistent id across a dozen tests that assert `no_such_item`, and a rule there
would change that code.

**Reads report, writes refuse.** `find_slice_file` returns `None` for an unusable id
rather than raising — `verify` exists to describe broken state and must not die on the
state it is describing. The first version raised there and made `verify` exit 2 instead of
reporting; a test caught it.

**Case collision, folded in.** `allocate` compared exactly, so `S01` and `s01` were two
index rows and one file on a case-insensitive filesystem, the second silently overwriting
the first. Now refused, with its own message and code — "already exists" would have been
untrue, since `s01` genuinely was not in the index.

**Deviation from the plan.** The plan called for resolve-and-compare containment in
`slice_path`. Not done, and the reason I first gave for dropping it was wrong: I measured
a suite slowdown and blamed the resolve, then found by stashing that the slowdown predated
the change entirely. The real argument is simpler — the plan was contrasting resolve
against *string-matching on `..`*, but the rule here is an allowlist that admits no path
separator at all, so a valid id is always a single component and the join provably cannot
leave the folder. Resolve would only add symlink checking on slicer's own directory.

**Not in this slice:** unicode in ids. The rule is ASCII, which is what every scheme
slicer generates produces.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Every id in the Why section is refused, and `migrate` refuses the tree.
